entry.evidence: However, the study of hydrodiversity has been much less developed than other aspects of the geological heritage

steps.action: States the aim of contributing an inclusive definition of hydrodiversity by explaining the hydrogeochemical processes behind diverse water features and their services.
steps.quote: The objective of this work is to help with an inclusive definition of hydrodiversity

steps.action: Selects the Los Hoyos evaporitic karst enclave, with springs, wetlands and leakages ranging from fresh to brine water, as the natural case study.
steps.quote: we have selected as a study area an evaporitic karst enclave of great geomorphological and environmental value located in southern Spain

steps.action: Records lake stage and spring level/flow (2013-2017), samples springs, leakages, wetlands and rain biweekly or once, with field EC, T, pH, DO, ion chromatography and water isotopes (CRDS or IRMS).
steps.quote: Samples for hydrochemical analysis were collected biweekly from the Aguileras, Fuente Camacho I and Fuente Camacho II outlets

steps.action: Checks chemical data quality with the charge balance error and discards samples above 5% (10% for brines); mean CBE 2.4%.
steps.quote: Any samples with CBE higher than 5% were discarded, or up to 10% for brine waters (i.e., M2 and R1).

steps.action: Converts brine isotope data from activity to concentration scale with the Sofer and Gat correction and uses PHREEQC with the PITZER database for molalities and saturation states.
steps.quote: data from activity scale to concentration scale was done using the

steps.action: Describes the declining spring discharge and lake stage over the record and fits a logarithmic stage-discharge relation that extrapolates to null flow near the spring elevation.
steps.quote: The combined evolution of both data series described a logarithmic regression

steps.action: Classifies waters into calcium-bicarbonate, calcium-sulfate and sodium-chloride facies, with mineralization (EC 0.4 to 220 mS/cm) rising toward lower altitudes.
steps.quote: Based on their hydrochemical composition, three different groups of water can be distinguished

steps.action: Runs a PCA on 10 variables and 158 observations; F1 (71.5%) reads as groundwater mineral evolution and F2 (16.9%) as surface-water evolution.
steps.quote: a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was carried out using the 10 variables included in Table 2

steps.action: Compares molar ratios (Na/Cl, HCO3/Ca, SO4/Ca, ions vs Cl, Cl/Br) with stoichiometric dissolution lines and cited Cl/Br ranges to identify halite, gypsum and calcite dissolution and evaporative precipitation.
steps.quote: following the typical 1:1 stoichiometric line that defines the NaCl (halite) dissolution reaction

steps.action: Computes mineral saturation indexes and pCO2 with PHREEQC-Pitzer: wetlands oversaturated in dolomite and calcite, brines near halite saturation, most waters near gypsum equilibrium.
steps.quote: The highest mineral saturation indexes (SI) correspond to dolomite

steps.action: Compares measured NaCl vs CaSO4 with the published CaSO4 solubility curve as a function of NaCl, finding excess CaSO4 in the wetlands and ionic-strength-enhanced solubility in brines.
steps.quote: together with the line of evolution of CaSO4 solubility as a function of the mass of NaCl dissolved in water

steps.action: Reports δ18O, δ2H and deuterium excess: brines near meteoric values, lakes with always negative d-excess, and samples aligned on evaporation lines.
steps.quote: Waters from the Grande and Chica lakes always have negative values of d

steps.action: Compares the fitted evaporation slopes (4.66 for lakes, 2.35 for the spring) with reference slopes for free-surface versus subsurface evaporation.
steps.quote: according to the slope calculated by linear fit (2.35), would have taken place in the subsurface rather than in free surface water

steps.action: Simulates with Gonfiantini's method the chemical and isotopic evaporation paths of rainwater (A) and of two spring samples (B, C), the expectations of rain-fed versus groundwater-fed wetlands.
steps.quote: The theoretical chemical and isotopic evolution of rainwater (A) and two of the samples from the Aguileras spring (B and C)

steps.action: Finds the Grande and Chica lake samples near the spring-water evaporation lines and the Vizcaíno sample near the rainwater line.
steps.quote: samples scatter close to the evaporation lines simulated from the spring water (B and C)

steps.action: Compares the lagged, attenuated lake-stage response with rainfall to infer groundwater input to Grande lake, in agreement with earlier studies.
steps.quote: All this evidences water input in the water balance of the wetland other than precipitation and runoff

steps.action: Computes the lake-level decline expected if evaporation were the only outflow (3320 mm) against the observed 4150 mm.
steps.quote: if evaporation were the only wetland outflow, the theoretical descent would have been 3320 mm

steps.action: Rejects evaporation as the sole outflow and concludes that groundwater outflow takes part in the Grande lake budget.
steps.quote: Hence, groundwater outflow must also participate in the Grande lake water budget.

steps.action: Poses the rival that the nearby, lower Aguileras spring is fed directly by Grande lake.
steps.quote: could suggest a hydrogeological connection between them

steps.action: Compares lake and spring isotopic signatures and evaporation slopes, which differ, as earlier works also found.
steps.quote: However, the isotopic signatures of their waters are clearly different

steps.action: Excludes a direct lake-to-spring connection as the main source of spring water, also citing the hydraulic gradient direction and the smooth hydrograph.
steps.quote: the water drained by the outlet cannot come from the wetland, at least to a large extent

steps.action: Refines the account: the lake and the spring both drain the same aquifer, which explains their hydrodynamic correlation without a direct connection.
steps.quote: both drain the same hydrogeological system

steps.action: Checks the isotope-based interpretation against the independent major-ion covariation lines (Ca, Mg, SO4 vs Cl) that intersect the spring samples.
steps.quote: Therefore, hydrogeochemistry reinforce the interpretation made based on the isotopic data.

steps.action: Keeps the claim that groundwater inputs sustain the water table of both permanent lakes.
steps.quote: Thus, groundwater inputs are essential to maintain the water table in both the Grande and [...] .

steps.action: Reconstructs the western-sector processes: recharge, mineral dissolution, evapoconcentration in the lakes, gypsum precipitation and calcite precipitation enhanced by the common-ion effect.
steps.quote: All this suggests that Ca2+ is being removed from the solution by calcite precipitation.

steps.action: Uses travertine deposits at the lakes' overflow thresholds and at a capture doline as an independent trace of past overflow and calcite precipitation.
steps.quote: In fact, travertine deposits are found by the overflowing threshold of the wetlands

steps.action: Takes from the authors' earlier dating study the result that eastern brine groundwater is older than the spring water.
steps.quote: has proved that part of the groundwater drained through this sector is older than the Aguilera spring water

steps.action: Reconstructs the eastern brine evolution: long flowpaths through the saline core, halite dissolution, ionic-strength-enhanced gypsum solubility, calcite and halite precipitation at the outlets.
steps.quote: The mineralization of the brine groundwater is associated with high ionic strengths, which increase the solubility of gypsum

steps.action: Keeps the conclusion that geodiversity (lithology, karst forms, residence time, flowpath) conditions the area's hydrodiversity, chiefly chemically.
steps.quote: Therefore, in Los Hoyos area, geodiversity conditions hydrodiversity, mainly from a chemical standpoint.

steps.action: Maps the water features and processes onto Gray's geodiversity value categories using ecological, archaeological and administrative literature.
steps.quote: According to Gray (2005), humankind should protect geodiversity against hazardous anthropogenic activities because of its intrinsic, cultural, aesthetic, economic, functional, and scientific values.

steps.action: Refines the earlier definition of hydrodiversity (Gil-Márquez et al., 2022) into a set of water manifestations assessed by typology, natural variations and causal processes.
steps.quote: hydrodiversity could be described as the set of natural water manifestations that exist in an area, continental or marine, surface or groundwater

tree.answer: Yes: diverse water features from fresh to brine in one karst enclave
Partly: chemistry and isotopes measured; processes inferred
Explain processes behind hydrodiversity and define the term
Few, local: rain- vs groundwater-fed wetlands; direct lake-spring link vs shared aquifer; evaporation-only outflow
Yes for local rivals: simulated evaporation lines, isotope slopes, water budget
Found: natural field site, no conditions set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Repeated biweekly sampling over four years at several water points
Partly: ion covariation supports isotopes; travertines support calcite precipitation
Conceptual model of five processes kept as best explanation

end.claim: Five processes (mineral availability, groundwater residence time, wetland evaporation, common-ion effect, high ionic strength), all tied to the area's geodiversity, explain the hydrodiversity of Los Hoyos.

decisive_move.sentence: Without reconstructing the hydrogeochemical processes from molar ratios, saturation indexes and isotopes, there would be no process-based account of the hydrodiversity.

gates.evidence: Sampling was a general monitoring routine (2013-2017) not directed by a stated hypothesis. Local rivals (direct lake-spring link, evaporation-only outflow, rain-fed wetlands) faced tests they could have failed (isotope signatures, water budget, simulated evaporation lines), but the headline five-process claim and the definition faced no failable test. Nothing was fixed before the data.

limits: The supplied XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps are cited by PDF/printed page. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The headline claim (five processes; geodiversity conditions hydrodiversity) is stated without explicit rivals, so it is a best explanation within an unstated rival set. The proposed definition of hydrodiversity is a synthesis proposal with no test (status none). Sub-claims: no direct lake-to-spring connection (best_explanation; isotopes plus gradient); groundwater inputs sustain the lakes (best_explanation; two independent lines of evidence); stage-discharge logarithmic relation (regularity_in_range for 2014-2017 only, no uncertainty given). The Fig. 2B legend reads 'Exponential fit' while the text says logarithmic; the paper does not resolve this. Vizcaíno (H3) and Tunel (R2) rest on single samples, and brine δ2H on n = 3, yet both carry interpretive weight. No uncertainties are reported for saturation indexes, evaporation-line simulations or slopes. Inference: the monitoring data likely overlap the first author's thesis (Gil-Márquez, 2018) and earlier papers; the paper does not state which analyses are new. The order of analysis cannot be told from the text.

disagreements.target: Regional geodiversity assessments (Araujo and Pereira, 2018; Bétard et al., 2018; Bétard and Peulvast, 2019; Fernández et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: The paper argues these assessments count aquifers only, and uses its case study to show that water quality, processes and related features carry diversity.
disagreements.quote: they only consider the existence of aquifers, but not their typology, the water quality, the hydrogeochemical processes

disagreements.support: Examples of hydrodynamic responses, tides and waves, and freeze-thaw, plus the Los Hoyos processes, motivate a broader definition.
disagreements.quote: However, the variety of water elements goes beyond their typology or physicochemical characteristics.

disagreements.target: Common practice of justifying geological protected areas by lithological, mineral, geomorphological or paleontological diversity
disagreements.support: Cites Ruban (2019) and then documents the natural and cultural heritage tied to water at Los Hoyos.
disagreements.quote: hydrology and hydrogeology are often secondary elements in geological protected areas, although they can bring as much attention as the other mentioned aspects

disagreements.target: Literature linking travertines mainly to carbonated springs and fluvial waterfalls (e.g., Collados-Lara et al., 2021; Florsheim et al., 2013)
disagreements.support: Reports travertines at wetland overflow thresholds and brine outlets, explained by calcite precipitation through the common-ion effect.
disagreements.quote: the appearance of travertines in the overflow area of wetlands, as observed in Grande and Chica lakes, is not well documented in the literature
